_doc: The forecaster's chart challenge (core/forecasting.gd). charts: practice synoptic situations. centre: low or high; bearing: where the centre lies from Britain (north, north-east ... north-west, or over); spacing: how tight the isobars are (tight, moderate, loose); front: the front nearest Britain (none, warm, cold); air: moist or dry. The wind is never stored: it follows from centre and bearing (Buys Ballot's law), and `weather` must match Forecasting.rule_weather so the data cannot contradict the rules. today: the chart behind each of the game's real weathers, matching the Shipping Forecast synopses in world/forecast.gd.

charts.title: A deep low out at Rockall
charts.why_wind: Air flows anticlockwise round a low in the northern hemisphere. With the low out to the north-west, the air over Britain comes from the south-west. Buys Ballot's law: stand with your back to the wind and the low is on your left.
charts.why_weather: The isobars are packed tight. A big change in pressure over a short distance means strong wind, and force 8 on the Beaufort scale is a gale. The cold front behind it will bring squalls too.

charts.title: A warm front from the west
charts.why_wind: The low is due west, so Britain sits on its eastern flank. Anticlockwise flow there runs from south to north: a southerly.
charts.why_weather: At a warm front, warm air slides gently up and over the colder air ahead of it. That makes thick layered cloud and hours of grey, steady light rain or drizzle, then it turns milder behind.

charts.title: A cold front sweeps through
charts.why_wind: With the low to the north, Britain is on its southern side. Anticlockwise round the low, the air there moves west to east: a westerly.
charts.why_weather: At a cold front, cold dense air undercuts the warm air and shoves it upwards fast. Tall cloud, heavy showers, sometimes thunder, then brighter and fresher behind. Short, sharp and very wet.

charts.title: A winter high over the Norwegian Sea
charts.why_wind: Air flows clockwise round a high. With the high to the north, the air over Britain comes from the east, straight off a frozen continent. Back to the wind, the high is on your right.
charts.why_weather: Under a high the air sinks, so cloud dries out and the sky clears. On a clear, calm winter night the ground's heat escapes straight up into space and the temperature drops below freezing: a hard frost.

charts.title: The Azores high in July
charts.why_wind: Clockwise round a high to the south-west puts a gentle north-westerly over Britain. The isobars are far apart, so it is only a breeze.
charts.why_weather: Sinking air under a high means few clouds and no rain. In summer that is a settled, sunny spell, and the longer it sits there, the hotter it gets.

charts.title: A high parked over Britain in November
charts.why_wind: Right under the centre of a high the isobars are far apart and the air hardly moves at all: light and variable.
charts.why_weather: Sinking air traps damp near the ground, and a still, cold night turns it to fog. A grey high that will not shift is what forecasters call anticyclonic gloom. It can last a week.

charts.title: A low over Biscay
charts.why_wind: A low to the south puts Britain on its northern flank. Anticlockwise round the low, the air up here comes from the east.
charts.why_weather: The warm front on its northern edge brings steady rain and drizzle for hours. In winter the same chart often means snow on the cold side of the front.

charts.title: A low heading off to Norway
charts.why_wind: Once a low has passed to the north-east, Britain is on its south-western flank. Anticlockwise flow there comes from the north-west: colder air, pulled down from the Arctic.
charts.why_weather: The cold front trails behind the low and sweeps through: squally showers of rain and hail, with cold bright gaps between them.

charts.title: A high over the continent in July
charts.why_wind: Clockwise round a high to the east drags air up from the south on its western flank: a southerly, and a warm one.
charts.why_weather: A southerly on the edge of a continental high carries hot air from Spain and France straight to Britain. A setup like this fed the UK's hottest day, 19 July 2022.

charts.title: A clear winter high to the west
charts.why_wind: On the eastern flank of a high the clockwise flow runs north to south: a northerly, down from the Arctic.
charts.why_weather: Clear skies and a light northerly on a winter night: the ground loses its heat and a hard frost sets in by morning. Scrape the car.

charts.title: Fog under a high over Dogger
charts.why_wind: A high to the east, over the North Sea, turns the air clockwise so that it reaches Britain from the south. Light, because the isobars are so far apart.
charts.why_weather: Mild damp air drifting slowly over cold ground and a cold sea: fog, and under a high nothing stirs it. The east coast gets the sea fog the locals call fret or haar.

charts.title: A violent low west of Ireland
charts.why_wind: The low is due west, so the anticlockwise flow over Britain comes from the south. Buys Ballot again: back to a southerly, the low is on your left, out to the west.
charts.why_weather: 968 millibars and isobars almost touching. That is force 9 or 10, a severe gale or storm. The Shipping Forecast would open with warnings of gales in every western sea area.

clear.title: Today's chart
clear.why_wind: Clockwise round a high to the south-west: a light north-westerly over Britain.
clear.why_weather: A fair-weather high: sinking air, broken cloud and nothing much falling. Dry, if not exactly tropical.

sunshine.title: Today's chart
sunshine.place: Fair Isle, with a ridge across the whole country
sunshine.why_wind: A ridge of high pressure lies right across Britain, so the isobars are wide apart and the wind is light and variable.
sunshine.why_weather: Dry sinking air across the whole country: wall-to-wall sunshine. Enjoy it, it will not last.

drizzle.title: Today's chart
drizzle.why_wind: A low out to the west over Shannon: anticlockwise flow puts a southerly over Britain.
drizzle.why_weather: Its warm front is crossing the country, so it is grey and damp: drizzle for most of the day.

downpour.title: Today's chart
downpour.why_wind: A deepening low to the north-west: anticlockwise flow means a south-westerly over Britain.
downpour.why_weather: The cold front is on top of us. Heavy rain, then showers behind it. It is tipping it down.

fog.title: Today's chart
fog.why_wind: A high sitting over Dogger, to the east: a light southerly drifts up on its western side.
fog.why_weather: Damp, still air under a stationary high: fog, and nothing to move it on.

gale.title: Today's chart
gale.trend: deepening rapidly, expected Fair Isle 968 by midnight
gale.why_wind: A rapidly deepening low to the north-west: a south-westerly, and a strong one.
gale.why_weather: The isobars are almost touching. Gale force 8 at least, severe gale 9 in the west. Hold on to your hat.

frost.title: Today's chart
frost.why_wind: A big high over Scandinavia to the north: clockwise flow sends an easterly across Britain, bitterly cold.
frost.why_weather: Clear skies, dry continental air and a bitter easterly: a hard frost underfoot.
